action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"); Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".

- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Vous avez raison, et ma liste était trompeuse sur ce point. J'ai vérifié les fichiers.

**Ce qui existe déjà :**
- `loop_benchy_upsidedown_tilted_apex_layers_pass4.gif` montre les couches Bird dans leur ordre d'impression. Cet ordre vient de l'étape 5 et suit l'arbre : disque, pilier, cabine, puis la coque en partant de la cabine, déposée en dernier. C'est le GIF que vous avez validé.
- `..._deformed_slice_pass4_toolpaths_*.png` montre les trajectoires complètes (parois et remplissage) ramenées dans la pièce réelle. Ce sont des images fixes.

**Deux nuances :**
1. Le GIF date de la première tentative (`bird_to_apex.py`, 284 couches). Il ne montre que les **contours** des couches, pas le remplissage. La version finale, avec parois et remplissage, n'a pas encore de GIF, mais le script existant peut en faire un.
2. L'**ordre des couches** est donc bien obtenu. Ce que j'appelais « étape 7 », c'est l'ordonnancement par couleur et le choix entre trou et purge. Sans peinture, il se réduit à une passe par couche dans l'ordre déjà calculé : c'est une formalité, pas un chantier.

**Le vrai travail restant de ce côté est donc l'étape 8 :**
- passer chaque point dans le repère machine ;
- calculer l'inclinaison de la tête à partir de ∇φ dans la pièce réelle, dans la plage 0 à 185° ;
- lisser les angles dans le temps.

Ensuite viennent les trajets à vide, puis la mesure step9b.

    # --- verification 1 : planeite, recouvrement ------------------------------
    spread = np.array([np.ptp(np.vstack(L.contour_3d)[:, 2]) for L in layers if L.contour_3d])
    from collections import Counter
    from shapely.validation import explain_validity
    reasons, invalid = Counter(), 0
    for L in layers:
        bad = [explain_validity(Polygon(c[:, :2])) for c in L.contour_3d if len(c) >= 3]
        bad = [r.split("[")[0].strip() for r in bad if r != "Valid Geometry"]
        invalid += bool(bad)
        reasons.update(bad)
    print(f"planeite : ecart en z max par couche = {spread.max():.1e} mm ; "
          f"couches avec un contour invalide : {invalid}/{len(layers)} (avant : 65/284) ; "
          f"raisons : {dict(reasons)}")

    # --- verification 2 : remplissage mesure / attendu ------------------------
    ratios, split_pieces, empty_pieces, holes_total, holes_bordered = [], 0, 0, 0, 0
    for L in layers:
        # dans le REPERE LOCAL de la couche, celui de toolpath_2d (origine et
        # axes propres a chaque couche, meme si le plan est horizontal)
        loops = [_project_to_local_2d(np.asarray(c), L.local_frame) for c in L.contour_3d if len(c) >= 3]
        polys = material_polygons(loops) if loops else []
        area = sum(p.area for p in polys)
        tp = L.toolpath_2d or []
        lengths = [np.linalg.norm(np.diff(t[:, :2], axis=0), axis=1).sum() for t in tp]
        infill = sum(l for t, l in zip(tp, lengths) if len(t) == 2)
        walls = sum(lengths) - infill
        expected = max(0.0, area - walls * w) * density / w
        if expected > 20.0:          # couches ou du remplissage est attendu
            ratios.append(infill / expected)
        # Couverture (defauts corriges le 2026-09-26 dans _offset_walls) :
        #  - chaque morceau d'une zone coupee en deux par la 1re paroi doit
        #    contenir de la trajectoire ;
        #  - chaque trou doit etre borde par son contour.
        from shapely.geometry import MultiPoint
        tp_pts = MultiPoint(np.vstack([t[:, :2] for t in tp])) if tp else None
        for p in polys:
            g = p.buffer(-w, join_style="mitre")
            if g.geom_type == "MultiPolygon":
                for q in g.geoms:
                    if q.area > 0.5:
                        split_pieces += 1
                        empty_pieces += tp_pts is None or not q.buffer(1e-6).intersects(tp_pts)
        # trous : sur les boucles BRUTES, telles que l'etape 6 les recoit (la
        # reparation buffer(0) des boucles qui se croisent cree de faux trous
        # et deplace les sommets)
        if tp and loops:
            tree = cKDTree(np.vstack([t[:, :2] for t in tp]))
            for _outer, holes in _classify_contours(loops):
                for hole in holes:
                    holes_total += 1
                    holes_bordered += (tree.query(hole[:, :2])[0] < 1e-6).mean() >= 0.95
    ratios = np.array(ratios)
    print(f"remplissage mesure / attendu, sur {len(ratios)} couches qui en attendent : "
          f"mediane {np.median(ratios):.2f}, 10e-90e centiles {np.percentile(ratios, 10):.2f}-"
          f"{np.percentile(ratios, 90):.2f} (couche 185 avant : 0,27)")
    print(f"morceaux (zone coupee par la 1re paroi, > 0,5 mm2) : {split_pieces}, "
          f"dont SANS trajectoire : {empty_pieces}")
    print(f"trous : {holes_total}, bordes par leur contour : {holes_bordered}")

    # --- retour dans la piece reelle ------------------------------------------
    back = DeformedToOriginal(cells, pk, p0)
    out_layers, n_pts, n_out, n_amb, all_contour = [], 0, 0, 0, []
    for L in layers:
        tp3 = []
        for t in (L.toolpath_2d or []):
            mapped, _, score, containing = back(_lift_to_3d(np.asarray(t), L.local_frame))
            n_pts += len(mapped)
            n_out += int((score < -1e-6).sum())
            n_amb += int((containing >= 2).sum())
            tp3.append(mapped + offset)
        contours = [back(np.asarray(c))[0] + offset for c in L.contour_3d]
        all_contour.extend(contours)
        out_layers.append({"contour_3d": contours, "isovalue": L.isovalue,
                           "toolpath_2d": [np.asarray(t) for t in (L.toolpath_2d or [])],
                           "toolpath_3d": tp3})
    print(f"retour : {n_pts} points, hors de tout tetraedre {n_out} ({n_out / n_pts:.2%}), "
          f"ambigus (plissement) {n_amb} ({n_amb / n_pts:.2%})")

    original = trimesh.load(stl)
    pts = np.vstack(all_contour)
    pts = pts[np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(pts), min(20000, len(pts)), replace=False)]
    _, dist, _ = trimesh.proximity.closest_point(original, pts)
    print(f"contours ramenes -> surface du STL d'origine : mediane {np.median(dist):.3f} mm, "
          f"95e centile {np.percentile(dist, 95):.3f} mm, max {dist.max():.3f} mm")

    out = f"{prefix}_deformed_slice_pass{pass_index}.pkl"
    with open(out, "wb") as f:
        pickle.dump(out_layers, f)
    print(f"sortie : {out}")

J'ai ouvert le GIF dans votre visionneuse. Il montre parois et remplissage dans l'ordre d'impression : les couches déposées vont du bleu au jaune, et la couche en cours de dépôt est en blanc.
[loop_benchy_upsidedown_tilted_deformed_slice_pass4_toolpaths.gif](research/S4_Slicer/output_models/loop_benchy_upsidedown_tilted_deformed_slice_pass4_toolpaths.gif)

**En faisant le GIF, j'ai trouvé et corrigé un défaut** dans `bird_slice_deformed.py`, qui reste en local :
- **Le problème :** une ligne de remplissage n'a que deux points. Seules ses deux extrémités étaient ramenées dans la pièce réelle, puis reliées par une droite. Or une droite dans l'espace déformé devient une courbe dans la pièce réelle. Ces droites coupaient donc à travers la coque au lieu de suivre la couche, jusqu'à 39 mm de long. Les images d'hier avaient ce défaut, mais il ne se voyait pas à cette échelle.
- **La correction :** chaque trajectoire est découpée en pas d'au plus 0,5 mm avant d'être ramenée. Sur l'image à 75 %, le remplissage de la couche blanche épouse maintenant la courbure de la coque.

**Ce qui reste, et que je n'ai pas corrigé :**
- 481 segments sur 250 000 (0,19 %, sur 66 couches) font encore plus de 2 mm, jusqu'à 15 mm.
- Ce sont des sauts, pas des cordes. Là où la déformation fait un pli, l'espace déformé se recouvre. Deux points voisins de la trajectoire sont alors attribués à deux épaisseurs différentes de la pièce.
- La correction serait de choisir le tétraèdre par continuité : prendre celui qui touche le tétraèdre du point précédent. Il faudra le faire avant l'étape 8, sinon ces sauts deviendront de vrais mouvements de la machine.

Dites-moi ce que vous pensez de l'ordre de dépôt dans le GIF.

def _generate_infill(
    boundary: Polygon,
    density: float,
    pattern: InfillPattern,
    nozzle_width: float,
    sweep_angle_rad: float = 0.0,
) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """
    Genere l'infill a l'interieur de `boundary` par un balayage de lignes
    paralleles, clippees par le polygone (shapely.intersection). L'espacement
    entre lignes vaut nozzle_width / density : 1.0 = lignes jointives (une
    largeur de buse), 0.2 = une ligne toutes les cinq largeurs de buse -
    premiere passe simple, suffisante pour l'objectif actuel (pas
    d'optimisation de trajet).

    Correction (2026-09-26) : l'espacement etait derive de la TAILLE de la
    couche (`diagonal / density * 0.05`), jamais de la buse - si bien qu'une
    couche de 35 mm a 20 % recevait une ligne tous les 8,75 mm au lieu de
    2 mm, et que plus une couche etait grande, plus elle etait creuse.
    Mesure sur les couches Bird du Benchy (43 mm de remplissage au lieu
    d'environ 160 sur une couche de 424 mm2).

    sweep_angle_rad force l'orientation du balayage (utilise pour les ponts,
    cf. Decision 2 du plan : traverser perpendiculairement a la portee).
    """
    if boundary is None or boundary.is_empty or density <= 0:
        return []

    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = boundary.bounds
    diagonal = float(np.hypot(maxx - minx, maxy - miny))
    if diagonal <= 0:
        return []

    spacing = nozzle_width / min(density, 1.0)
    # borne basse pour eviter un nombre de lignes explosif (buse ou densite
    # aberrante) : le balayage couvre 2 x diagonal, donc au plus
    # _MAX_INFILL_LINES lignes par couche.
    spacing = max(spacing, 2.0 * diagonal / _MAX_INFILL_LINES, 1e-6)

    center = np.array([(minx + maxx) / 2.0, (miny + maxy) / 2.0])
    half_extent = diagonal  # sur-couvre largement pour rester valide apres rotation

    lines: list[np.ndarray] = []
    offsets = np.arange(-half_extent, half_extent, spacing)
    cos_a, sin_a = np.cos(sweep_angle_rad), np.sin(sweep_angle_rad)
    direction = np.array([cos_a, sin_a])
    perpendicular = np.array([-sin_a, cos_a])

    for offset in offsets:
        base = center + perpendicular * offset
        p0 = base - direction * half_extent
        p1 = base + direction * half_extent
        segment = LineString([p0, p1])
        clipped = segment.intersection(boundary)
        if clipped.is_empty:
            continue
        if clipped.geom_type == "LineString":
            coords = np.asarray(clipped.coords)
            if len(coords) >= 2:
                lines.append(coords)
        elif clipped.geom_type == "MultiLineString":
            for part in clipped.geoms:
                coords = np.asarray(part.coords)
                if len(coords) >= 2:
                    lines.append(coords)

    return lines

Les réglages utilisés sont les réglages par défaut d'Apex (`Step6Params`, repris par `main.PipelineParams`) :

| paramètre | valeur |
|---|---|
| buse | 0,4 mm |
| parois | 2 |
| densité de remplissage | 20 %, soit une ligne tous les 2 mm |
| motif | lignes parallèles (`LINES`) |

En relisant `_generate_infill` pour vous répondre, j'ai trouvé trois manques dans l'étape 6 d'Apex. Ils expliquent l'aspect timide autant que les 20 % :

1. **Le motif est ignoré.** Le paramètre `pattern` est reçu mais jamais lu. `GRID` existe dans l'énumération, mais seules des lignes sont produites.
2. **Toutes les couches ont la même orientation.** L'angle vaut 0° partout, sauf sur les ponts. Les lignes s'empilent donc les unes sur les autres sans jamais se croiser d'une couche à la suivante, ce qui donne un remplissage sans tenue. Un slicer classique alterne à 90° d'une couche à l'autre, ou passe à une grille, des triangles ou du gyroïde.
3. **Il n'y a pas de peaux pleines dessus et dessous.** Apex ne dépose aucune couche pleine (à 100 %) sur les faces supérieures et inférieures. Le dessus de la coque se referme donc avec seulement 20 % de lignes, ce qui n'est pas imprimable proprement.

En plus, chaque ligne de remplissage est une polyligne séparée de deux points, reliée à la suivante par un trajet à vide. Ce n'est pas faux, mais c'est très lent à imprimer.

Ce sont des défauts d'Apex, pas de la méthode Bird : on les verrait aussi sur le pipeline actuel.

Je propose de corriger dans cet ordre :
1. alternance de l'angle entre couches, et `GRID` réellement branché (petit) ;
2. peaux pleines dessus et dessous, avec un nombre de couches réglable (plus gros, car il faut savoir quelles zones d'une couche sont proches d'une face exposée) ;
3. lignes reliées en zigzag.

Je commence par le premier point ?
Pour l'infill, faire des lignes Croisées-Alternées : une couche de zigzag horizontral, un couche de zigzag vertical, etc.

is_bridge_per_point = overhang_map.is_bridge[nearest_faces]
    ratio = float(is_bridge_per_point.mean()) if len(is_bridge_per_point) else 0.0
    if ratio < threshold:
        return None

    span_vectors = overhang_map.bridge_span_direction[nearest_faces[is_bridge_per_point]]
    valid = ~np.isnan(span_vectors).any(axis=1)
    if not np.any(valid):
        return None

    mean_span = span_vectors[valid].mean(axis=0)
    norm = np.linalg.norm(mean_span)
    if norm < 1e-12:
        return None
    mean_span = mean_span / norm

    _origin, axis_u, axis_v = local_frame
    span_2d = np.array([np.dot(mean_span, axis_u), np.dot(mean_span, axis_v)])
    span_norm = np.linalg.norm(span_2d)
    if span_norm < 1e-12:
        return None
    return span_2d / span_norm

        if not (7.0 <= z_mean <= 9.5):

        if not infill_lines:

"""
pipeline/step6_toolpath2d.py

Etape 6 du pipeline : remplissage 2D de chaque couche (parois + infill),
dans le repere local de la couche produit par step5.

Depend de Layer (step5, contour_3d + local_frame), MeshData (step1, kdtree
pour le pont surface/volume), OverhangMap (step2, is_bridge +
bridge_span_direction).

Ce que ce fichier fait, dans l'ordre, par Layer :
  1. Projette chaque boucle de contour_3d dans le plan local (local_frame).
  2. Classe les boucles projetees en contours "matiere" / trous par
     imbrication geometrique (point_in_polygon_2d), PAS par signe d'aire -
     voir CLAUDE.md limite #11 et la Decision 3bis de step5.
  3. Genere les parois par offset polygonal successif vers l'interieur
     (shapely.buffer), wall_count niveaux, en s'arretant proprement si
     l'offset fait disparaitre une zone trop fine avant d'atteindre
     wall_count.
  4. Genere l'infill a l'interieur du dernier offset.
  5. Pour les boucles associees a une zone is_bridge (step2, via le meme
     pont kdtree surface/volume que step4/step5) : ajoute des parois
     d'ancrage supplementaires sur le perimetre puis reoriente l'infill
     pour traverser perpendiculairement a bridge_span_direction.

Sortie : la meme liste de Layer, avec toolpath_2d rempli (repere local 2D,
pas 3D - step8 se chargera de le relever au repere machine).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from enum import Enum

import numpy as np
import shapely
import shapely.affinity
from shapely.geometry import LineString, MultiPolygon, Polygon

from core import _cpp
from core.geometry_utils import point_in_polygon_2d
from core.mesh_types import Layer, MeshData, OverhangMap


class ToolpathGenerationError(Exception):
    """Levee si une couche ne peut produire aucune trajectoire exploitable."""


class InfillPattern(Enum):
    LINES = "lines"
    GRID = "grid"


@dataclass
class Step6Params:
    nozzle_width: float = 0.4
    wall_count: int = 2
    infill_density: float = 0.2          # dans (0, 1]
    infill_pattern: InfillPattern = InfillPattern.LINES
    # seuil de PRESENCE (pas de majorite) : proportion minimale de points

''','''class InfillPattern(Enum):
    # lignes paralleles independantes, meme orientation a toutes les couches
    # (comportement historique)
    LINES = "lines"
    # deux balayages croises a 90 deg dans CHAQUE couche, chacun a la moitie

    GRID = "grid"
    # lignes croisees-alternees : un zigzag continu par zone, oriente selon
    # l'axe u du repere local une couche sur deux et selon l'axe v l'autre
    # (voir `_infill_angle_for_layer`)
    CROSSED_ZIGZAG = "crossed_zigzag"
''')

    # seuil de PRESENCE''')

old_start = s.index('def _generate_infill(')
old_end = s.index('# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Decision 2 - Pont surface')
new_fn = '''def _generate_infill(
    boundary: Polygon,
    density: float,
    pattern: InfillPattern,
    nozzle_width: float,
    sweep_angle_rad: float = 0.0,
) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """
    Genere l'infill a l'interieur de `boundary` par balayage de lignes
    paralleles clippees par le polygone (shapely.intersection), selon
    `pattern` :
      - LINES : lignes independantes (une polyligne de 2 points chacune),
        orientees selon `sweep_angle_rad` ;
      - GRID : deux balayages croises a 90 deg, chacun a densite / 2 ;
      - CROSSED_ZIGZAG : les lignes d'un meme balayage sont reliees bout a
        bout en zigzag (`_connect_zigzag`) ; l'alternance entre couches est
        portee par l'appelant via `sweep_angle_rad`
        (`_infill_angle_for_layer`).

    L'espacement entre lignes d'un balayage vaut nozzle_width / density :
    1.0 = lignes jointives (une largeur de buse), 0.2 = une ligne toutes les
    cinq largeurs de buse.

    Correction (2026-09-26) : l'espacement etait derive de la TAILLE de la
    couche (`diagonal / density * 0.05`), jamais de la buse - si bien qu'une
    couche de 35 mm a 20 % recevait une ligne tous les 8,75 mm au lieu de
    2 mm, et que plus une couche etait grande, plus elle etait creuse.
    Mesure sur les couches Bird du Benchy (43 mm de remplissage au lieu
    d'environ 160 sur une couche de 424 mm2). Et `pattern` etait recu sans
    jamais etre lu : GRID produisait des lignes simples.

    sweep_angle_rad force l'orientation du balayage (ponts : traverser
    perpendiculairement a la portee, cf. Decision 2 du plan ; couches
    normales en CROSSED_ZIGZAG : 0 ou pi/2 selon la couche).
    """
    if boundary is None or boundary.is_empty or density <= 0:
        return []

    if pattern is InfillPattern.GRID:
        half = min(density, 1.0) / 2.0
        return (
            _generate_infill(boundary, half, InfillPattern.LINES, nozzle_width, sweep_angle_rad)
            + _generate_infill(
                boundary, half, InfillPattern.LINES, nozzle_width, sweep_angle_rad + np.pi / 2.0
            )
        )

    scans, spacing = _clipped_scanlines(boundary, density, nozzle_width, sweep_angle_rad)
    if pattern is InfillPattern.CROSSED_ZIGZAG:
        return _connect_zigzag(scans, boundary, spacing)
    return [segment for scan in scans for segment in scan]


def _clipped_scanlines(
    boundary: Polygon, density: float, nozzle_width: float, sweep_angle_rad: float
) -> tuple[list[list[np.ndarray]], float]:
    """
    Lignes de balayage clippees par `boundary`, regroupees PAR ligne de
    balayage (dans l'ordre de balayage) et, au sein d'une ligne, triees et
    orientees dans le sens du balayage. Rend aussi l'espacement retenu.
    """
    minx, miny, maxx, maxy = boundary.bounds
    diagonal = float(np.hypot(maxx - minx, maxy - miny))
    if diagonal <= 0:
        return [], 0.0

    spacing = nozzle_width / min(density, 1.0)
    # borne basse pour eviter un nombre de lignes explosif (buse ou densite
    # aberrante) : le balayage couvre 2 x diagonal, donc au plus
    # _MAX_INFILL_LINES lignes par couche.
    spacing = max(spacing, 2.0 * diagonal / _MAX_INFILL_LINES, 1e-6)

    center = np.array([(minx + maxx) / 2.0, (miny + maxy) / 2.0])
    half_extent = diagonal  # sur-couvre largement pour rester valide apres rotation

    offsets = np.arange(-half_extent, half_extent, spacing)
    cos_a, sin_a = np.cos(sweep_angle_rad), np.sin(sweep_angle_rad)
    direction = np.array([cos_a, sin_a])
    perpendicular = np.array([-sin_a, cos_a])

    scans: list[list[np.ndarray]] = []
    for offset in offsets:
        base = center + perpendicular * offset
        p0 = base - direction * half_extent
        p1 = base + direction * half_extent
        clipped = LineString([p0, p1]).intersection(boundary)
        if clipped.is_empty:
            continue
        parts = clipped.geoms if hasattr(clipped, "geoms") else [clipped]
        segments = []
        for part in parts:
            if part.geom_type != "LineString":
                continue
            coords = np.asarray(part.coords)
            if len(coords) < 2:
                continue
            if np.dot(coords[-1] - coords[0], direction) < 0:
                coords = coords[::-1]
            segments.append(coords)
        if segments:
            segments.sort(key=lambda c: float(np.dot(c[0], direction)))
            scans.append(segments)
    return scans, spacing


def _connect_zigzag(
    scans: list[list[np.ndarray]], boundary: Polygon, spacing: float
) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """
    Relie les segments de lignes de balayage SUCCESSIVES en zigzag : depuis
    la fin d'un segment, on enchaine sur l'extremite la plus proche d'un
    segment libre de la ligne suivante, que l'on parcourt alors en sens
    inverse. Le raccord est un segment droit, accepte seulement s'il reste
    dans `boundary` (jamais a travers un trou ni hors de la zone a remplir)
    et s'il mesure au plus `_ZIGZAG_MAX_CONNECTOR_SPACINGS` espacements - au-dela
    il longerait un bord presque parallele au balayage et deposerait une
    ligne en trop. Sinon le zigzag s'arrete et un nouveau commence (une zone
    concave donne donc plusieurs zigzags, relies par des trajets a vide).
    """
    from shapely.prepared import prep

    inside = prep(boundary.buffer(max(1e-6, spacing * 1e-4)))
    max_connector = _ZIGZAG_MAX_CONNECTOR_SPACINGS * spacing
    used = [[False] * len(scan) for scan in scans]
    chains: list[np.ndarray] = []

    for k, scan in enumerate(scans):
        for j, segment in enumerate(scan):
            if used[k][j]:
                continue
            used[k][j] = True
            parts = [segment]
            end = segment[-1]
            current = k
            while current + 1 < len(scans):
                best = None
                for jj, candidate in enumerate(scans[current + 1]):
                    if used[current + 1][jj]:
                        continue
                    for reverse, start in ((False, candidate[0]), (True, candidate[-1])):
                        distance = float(np.linalg.norm(start - end))
                        if best is None or distance < best[0]:
                            best = (distance, jj, reverse)
                if best is None or best[0] > max_connector:
                    break
                distance, jj, reverse = best
                candidate = scans[current + 1][jj]
                start = candidate[-1] if reverse else candidate[0]
                if distance > 0 and not inside.covers(LineString([end, start])):
                    break
                used[current + 1][jj] = True
                oriented = candidate[::-1] if reverse else candidate
                parts.append(oriented)
                end = oriented[-1]
                current += 1
            chains.append(np.vstack(parts))
    return chains


def _infill_angle_for_layer(layer: Layer, isovalue_rank: dict) -> float:
    """
    Orientation du balayage d'une couche normale (hors pont) en
    CROSSED_ZIGZAG : axe u du repere local (0) une couche sur deux, axe v
    (pi/2) l'autre. La parite est prise sur le RANG de l'isovaleur, pas sur
    la position dans la liste : l'ordre d'impression (step5, en arbre) fait
    se succeder des couches de branches differentes, alors que deux couches
    EMPILEES ont des isovaleurs consecutives - ce sont elles qui doivent se
    croiser. Les morceaux d'une meme isovaleur (clusters) partagent donc la
    meme orientation. Sans isovaleur, repli sur l'identifiant de couche.
    """
    if layer.isovalue is not None and layer.isovalue in isovalue_rank:
        rank = isovalue_rank[layer.isovalue]
    else:
        rank = layer.id
    return 0.0 if rank % 2 == 0 else np.pi / 2.0


'''
s = s[:old_start] + new_fn + s[old_end:]

s=s.replace('''                infill = _generate_infill(
                    innermost, params.infill_density, params.infill_pattern, params.nozzle_width
                )

def _connect_zigzag(
    scans: list[list[np.ndarray]], boundary: Polygon, spacing: float
) -> list[np.ndarray]:
    """
    Relie les segments de lignes de balayage SUCCESSIVES en zigzag : depuis
    la fin d'un segment, on enchaine sur l'extremite la plus proche d'un
    segment libre de la ligne suivante, que l'on parcourt alors en sens
    inverse. Le raccord est un segment droit, accepte seulement s'il reste
    dans `boundary` (jamais a travers un trou ni hors de la zone a remplir)
    et s'il mesure au plus `_ZIGZAG_MAX_CONNECTOR_SPACINGS` espacements - au-dela
    il longerait un bord presque parallele au balayage et deposerait une
    ligne en trop. Sinon le zigzag s'arrete et un nouveau commence (une zone
    concave donne donc plusieurs zigzags, relies par des trajets a vide).
    """
    from shapely.prepared import prep

    inside = prep(boundary.buffer(max(1e-6, spacing * 1e-4)))
    max_connector = _ZIGZAG_MAX_CONNECTOR_SPACINGS * spacing
    used = [[False] * len(scan) for scan in scans]
    chains: list[np.ndarray] = []

    for k, scan in enumerate(scans):
        for j, segment in enumerate(scan):
            if used[k][j]:
                continue
            used[k][j] = True
            parts = [segment]
            end = segment[-1]
            current = k
            while current + 1 < len(scans):
                best = None
                for jj, candidate in enumerate(scans[current + 1]):
                    if used[current + 1][jj]:
                        continue
                    for reverse, start in ((False, candidate[0]), (True, candidate[-1])):
                        distance = float(np.linalg.norm(start - end))
                        if best is None or distance < best[0]:
                            best = (distance, jj, reverse)
                if best is None or best[0] > max_connector:
                    break
                distance, jj, reverse = best
                candidate = scans[current + 1][jj]
                start = candidate[-1] if reverse else candidate[0]
                if distance > 0 and not inside.covers(LineString([end, start])):
                    break
                used[current + 1][jj] = True
                oriented = candidate[::-1] if reverse else candidate
                parts.append(oriented)
                end = oriented[-1]
                current += 1
            chains.append(np.vstack(parts))
    return chains


def _infill_angle_for_layer(layer: Layer, isovalue_rank: dict) -> float:
    """
    Orientation du balayage d'une couche normale (hors pont) en
    CROSSED_ZIGZAG : axe u du repere local (0) une couche sur deux, axe v
    (pi/2) l'autre. La parite est prise sur le RANG de l'isovaleur, pas sur
    la position dans la liste : l'ordre d'impression (step5, en arbre) fait

content.text:
Le sens alterne bien. C'était le GIF qui trompait.

- **Les données alternent correctement.** Sur les 199 couches qui ont du remplissage, les 199 ont le bon sens : u, v, u, v… d'une couche empilée à la suivante.
- **Le GIF ne le montrait pas.** Il n'affichait qu'une couche sur deux, donc la couche en blanc était toujours de la même parité et balayait toujours dans le même sens. Il passe maintenant par une couche sur trois, et le sens alterne d'une image à l'autre. Je l'ai rouvert.

**Ce qui reste « bizarre » sur la planche, et pourquoi :**
1. **Des dents de scie dans les bandes étroites** (couches 242 et 128). La bande entre les parois ne fait que 1 à 2 mm de large, mais l'alternance impose le sens du balayage, parfois presque en travers de la bande. Les lignes sont alors très courtes et ce sont les raccords, le long du bord, qui dominent. Cura fait la même chose dans ce cas. Deux sorties possibles :
   - orienter le zigzag dans la longueur de la bande, en renonçant à l'alternance là seulement ;
   - ne pas mettre de remplissage dans une bande de moins de 2 ou 3 largeurs de buse, et la combler avec une paroi de plus.
2. **Presque pas de remplissage dans la coque** (couches 26 et 77). La coque est fine : trois passes de paroi la remplissent presque entièrement, et il ne reste que des bouts de bande. C'est normal pour une coque mince à cette échelle.
3. **Des contours extérieurs « ouverts »** (bord gauche de la couche 166). C'est seulement l'affichage : le contour d'origine est stocké sans son point de fermeture, et le script de rendu ne le referme pas. La trajectoire elle-même n'a pas de trou.

**Pour la question de départ, le remplissage timide :** 20 % reste une densité faible, et il n'y a toujours pas de peau pleine sur les dessus et dessous. Ce sera la prochaine correction à faire si vous voulez un Benchy qui se referme proprement.

import pickle

for number in indices:
    layer = layers[number - 1]
    polylines = [np.asarray(t)[:, :3] for t in layer["toolpath_3d"] if len(t) >= 2]

        cells.append(np.concatenate([[len(t)], np.arange(offset, offset + len(t))]))
        offset += len(t)
    lines = pv.PolyData(points, lines=np.concatenate(cells))

        if view == "iso":
            plotter.view_isometric()
        elif view == "xy":
            plotter.view_xy()
        else:
            plotter.view_xz()
        plotter.add_text(f"couche {number}/{len(layers)} ({view})", color="white", font_size=10)
        shots.append(plotter.screenshot(return_img=True))
        plotter.close()
    out = path.replace(".pkl", f"_layer{number}_in_part.png")

        coeur de deux tetraedres venus de deux epaisseurs differentes de la
        piece. Choisir point par point (le mieux contenu) fait alors sauter la
        trajectoire d'une epaisseur a l'autre (sauts de 2 a 15 mm mesures).
        Ici, candidats = tetraedres qui contiennent le point (ou, pour un
        point hors de tout tetraedre, ceux a `outside_margin` pres du moins
        exterieur) ; on retient la suite de candidats qui minimise la somme
        des distances entre points ramenes consecutifs (Viterbi, exact).
        """
        n = len(points)
        _, cand = self.tree.query(points, k=self.k)
        with np.errstate(all="ignore"):

            valid[none] = score[none] >= best - outside_margin
        containing = (score > 1e-6).sum(axis=1)

        cost = np.where(valid[0], 0.0, np.inf)
        back = np.zeros((n, self.k), dtype=np.int64)
        for i in range(1, n):
            step = np.linalg.norm(mapped[i - 1][:, None, :] - mapped[i][None, :, :], axis=2)  # (k,k)
            total = cost[:, None] + step
            back[i] = total.argmin(axis=0)
            cost = np.where(valid[i], total.min(axis=0), np.inf)

        des distances entre points ramenes consecutifs (Viterbi, exact).
        """
        n = len(points)
        _, cand = self.tree.query(points, k=self.k)
        with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
            bary = np.stack([barycentric(points, self.tets[cand[:, j]]) for j in range(self.k)], axis=1)
        score = np.nan_to_num(bary.min(axis=2), nan=-np.inf)                     # (n,k)
        mapped = np.einsum("njv,njvk->njk", bary, self.original[self.cells[cand]])  # (n,k,3)
        valid = score > -1e-6
        none = ~valid.any(axis=1)
        if none.any():
            best = score[none].max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
            valid[none] = score[none] >= best - outside_margin
        containing = (score > 1e-6).sum(axis=1)

        cost = np.where(valid[0], 0.0, np.inf)
        back = np.zeros((n, self.k), dtype=np.int64)
        for i in range(1, n):
            step = np.linalg.norm(mapped[i - 1][:, None, :] - mapped[i][None, :, :], axis=2)  # (k,k)
            total = cost[:, None] + step
            back[i] = total.argmin(axis=0)
            cost = np.where(valid[i], total.min(axis=0), np.inf)
        choice = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.int64)
        choice[-1] = int(cost.argmin())
        for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
            choice[i - 1] = back[i, choice[i]]
        rows = np.arange(n)
        return mapped[rows, choice], cand[rows, choice], score[rows, choice], containing

"""
GIF d'ordre d'impression des trajectoires (parois + remplissage) DANS la
piece d'origine affichee en transparence : le rendu fil de fer seul
(render_layers_gif.py) ne permet pas de juger si un morceau de trajectoire
appartient a la piece.

Couleurs : couches deposees du bleu (premiere) au jaune (derniere), couche en
cours de depot en blanc. Pas IMPAIR entre images, pour que le remplissage
croise-alterne se voie changer de sens d'une image a l'autre.

Usage : .venv/Scripts/python.exe render_part_gif.py <couches.pkl> <piece.stl> [azimut] [elevation]
"""
import pickle
import sys

import numpy as np
import pyvista as pv
from PIL import Image

FIRST_COLOR = np.array([0x00, 0x00, 0xFF])
LAST_COLOR = np.array([0xFF, 0xF7, 0x00])

path, stl = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
azimuth = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else -30.0
elevation = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 20.0
layers = pickle.load(open(path, "rb"))
total = len(layers)
stride = max(1, total // 90)
if stride % 2 == 0:
    stride += 1


def layer_polydata(indices):
    """Lignes des couches `indices`, avec une couleur RGB par cellule."""
    points, cells, colors, offset = [], [], [], 0
    for i in indices:
        color = FIRST_COLOR + (LAST_COLOR - FIRST_COLOR) * (i / max(total - 1, 1))
        for t in layers[i]["toolpath_3d"]:
            t = np.asarray(t)[:, :3]
            if len(t) < 2:
                continue
            points.append(t)
            cells.append(np.concatenate([[len(t)], np.arange(offset, offset + len(t))]))
            colors.append(color)
            offset += len(t)
    if not points:
        return None
    mesh = pv.PolyData(np.vstack(points), lines=np.concatenate(cells))
    mesh.cell_data["rgb"] = np.array(colors, dtype=np.uint8)
    return mesh


part = pv.read(stl)
plotter = pv.Plotter(off_screen=True, window_size=(800, 800))
plotter.set_background("black")
plotter.add_mesh(part, color="lightgray", opacity=0.15)
plotter.view_isometric()
plotter.camera.azimuth = azimuth
plotter.camera.elevation = elevation
plotter.camera.zoom(1.3)

frames, placed, current_actor = [], 0, None
shown = list(range(0, total, stride))
if shown[-1] != total - 1:
    shown.append(total - 1)
for i in shown:
    batch = layer_polydata(range(placed, i + 1))
    if batch is not None:
        plotter.add_mesh(batch, scalars="rgb", rgb=True, line_width=1)
    placed = i + 1
    if current_actor is not None:
        plotter.remove_actor(current_actor)
        current_actor = None
    current = layer_polydata([i]) if i != total - 1 else None
    if current is not None:
        current_actor = plotter.add_mesh(current, color="white", line_width=3)
    plotter.add_text(f"Couche {i + 1}/{total}", color="white", font_size=12, name="title")
    frames.append(Image.fromarray(plotter.screenshot(return_img=True)))
plotter.close()

out = path.replace(".pkl", "_in_part.gif")
frames[0].save(out, save_all=True, append_images=frames[1:], duration=100, loop=0)
for frac in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0):
    frames[int(frac * (len(frames) - 1))].save(path.replace(".pkl", f"_in_part_{int(frac * 100)}pct.png"))
print(f"GIF : {out}  ({len(frames)} images)")

"""
GIF d'ordre d'impression des trajectoires (parois + remplissage) DANS la
piece d'origine affichee en transparence : le rendu fil de fer seul
(render_layers_gif.py) ne permet pas de juger si un morceau de trajectoire
appartient a la piece.

Couleurs : couches deposees du bleu (premiere) au jaune (derniere), couche en
cours de depot en blanc. Pas IMPAIR entre images, pour que le remplissage
croise-alterne se voie changer de sens d'une image a l'autre.

Usage : .venv/Scripts/python.exe render_part_gif.py <couches.pkl> <piece.stl> [azimut] [elevation]
"""
import pickle
import sys

import numpy as np
import pyvista as pv
from PIL import Image

FIRST_COLOR = np.array([0x00, 0x00, 0xFF])
LAST_COLOR = np.array([0xFF, 0xF7, 0x00])

path, stl = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
azimuth = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else -30.0
elevation = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 20.0
layers = pickle.load(open(path, "rb"))
total = len(layers)
stride = max(1, total // 90)
if stride % 2 == 0:
    stride += 1


def layer_polydata(indices):
    """Lignes des couches `indices`, avec une couleur RGB par cellule."""
    points, cells, colors, offset = [], [], [], 0
    for i in indices:
        color = FIRST_COLOR + (LAST_COLOR - FIRST_COLOR) * (i / max(total - 1, 1))
        for t in layers[i]["toolpath_3d"]:
            t = np.asarray(t)[:, :3]
            if len(t) < 2:
                continue
            points.append(t)
            cells.append(np.concatenate([[len(t)], np.arange(offset, offset + len(t))]))
            colors.append(color)
            offset += len(t)
    if not points:
        return None
    mesh = pv.PolyData(np.vstack(points), lines=np.concatenate(cells))
    mesh.cell_data["rgb"] = np.array(colors, dtype=np.uint8)
    return mesh


part = pv.read(stl)
plotter = pv.Plotter(off_screen=True, window_size=(800, 800))
plotter.set_background("black")
plotter.add_mesh(part, color="lightgray", opacity=0.15)
plotter.view_isometric()
plotter.camera.azimuth = azimuth
plotter.camera.elevation = elevation
plotter.camera.zoom(1.3)

frames, placed, current_actor = [], 0, None
shown = list(range(0, total, stride))
if shown[-1] != total - 1:
    shown.append(total - 1)
for i in shown:
    batch = layer_polydata(range(placed, i + 1))
    if batch is not None:
        plotter.add_mesh(batch, scalars="rgb", rgb=True, line_width=1)
    placed = i + 1
    if current_actor is not None:
        plotter.remove_actor(current_actor)
        current_actor = None
    current = layer_polydata([i]) if i != total - 1 else None
    if current is not None:
        current_actor = plotter.add_mesh(current, color="white", line_width=3)
    plotter.add_text(f"Couche {i + 1}/{total}", color="white", font_size=12, name="title")
    frames.append(Image.fromarray(plotter.screenshot(return_img=True)))
plotter.close()

out = path.replace(".pkl", "_in_part.gif")
frames[0].save(out, save_all=True, append_images=frames[1:], duration=100, loop=0)
for frac in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0):
    frames[int(frac * (len(frames) - 1))].save(path.replace(".pkl", f"_in_part_{int(frac * 100)}pct.png"))
print(f"GIF : {out}  ({len(frames)} images)")

Les deux sont faits. J'ai ouvert le nouveau GIF : les trajectoires s'y déposent dans la pièce, affichée en transparence, et la couche en cours est en blanc.
[loop_benchy_upsidedown_tilted_deformed_slice_pass4_in_part.gif](research/S4_Slicer/output_models/loop_benchy_upsidedown_tilted_deformed_slice_pass4_in_part.gif)

**Correction du retour dans la pièce réelle** (`bird_slice_deformed.py`, en local) :

| mesure | avant | après |
|---|---:|---:|
| points hors de la pièce (> 0,3 mm) | 68, jusqu'à 4 mm | **0** (pire écart 0,15 mm) |
| segments extrudés de plus de 1 mm | 1 274 | **0** |
| segments extrudés de plus de 5 mm | 79 | **0** |

Il a fallu trois mécanismes, car il y avait trois causes distinctes :
1. **Choix du tétraèdre par continuité.** Dans un pli, un point est pris dans deux épaisseurs de la pièce. Au lieu de choisir point par point, je choisis pour toute la trajectoire la suite de tétraèdres qui donne le chemin le plus continu dans la pièce réelle (Viterbi). Cela a supprimé environ 70 % des sauts.
2. **Subdivision adaptative.** Là où la déformation a comprimé la pièce, un pas de 0,5 mm dans l'espace déformé couvrait plusieurs millimètres dans la pièce réelle. Tout segment trop long une fois ramené est maintenant recoupé.
3. **Coupure des fausses zones pleines.** La vraie cause des points hors de la pièce (couche 65) n'était pas un saut. Dans un pli, le contour de la couche se croise lui-même, et la réparation du polygone y crée de la « matière » là où il n'y a que du vide. Les points à plus d'une demi-largeur de cordon hors du volume (364 points, soit 0,14 %) ne sont plus déposés.

**Ce que cela coûte :**
- 99 sauts restants, qu'aucun des trois mécanismes ne résout, sont devenus des trajets à vide au lieu d'être extrudés ;
- un peu de matière n'est plus déposée à l'endroit exact des plis. C'est un symptôme des replis mineurs de la passe 4 (moins de 13,7 mm² selon le juge), pas un défaut du tranchage.

Rien de nouveau dans Apex lui-même pour cette étape. Le motif croisé-alterné (`pipeline/step6_toolpath2d.py`, 375/375 tests) et la mise à jour de `CLAUDE.md` attendent toujours d'être commités, quand vous voudrez.
